sections.title: Headline
sections.content: Two papers lead this week's shortlist: a verification-guided LLM pipeline for autonomous topology optimization, and a study of how backdoor behavior is inherited or learned in distilled language models.

sections.title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization
sections.problem: Moving a topology optimization problem from description to optimized result is slow, expert-dependent, and unreliable, requiring manually written and debugged solver code that often fails or yields incorrect results.
sections.method: Agent4FreeFem, an LLM-driven pipeline that converts a natural-language problem description into verified optimization results, keeping the problem definition unmodified, localizing errors via independent evidence sources, and performing constrained automatic repairs.
sections.key_result: On a suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems, every case passed runtime verification and finished within each stage's repair budget.
sections.caveat: Results are reported on the authors' own problem suite; no external baselines or quantitative accuracy metrics are given in the abstract, and the organization attribution is only probable.
sections.why_it_matters: It targets end-to-end automation of an expert-heavy engineering design workflow while emphasizing verifiable outputs rather than unverified generation.

sections.title: Inherited or Learned? Backdoor Selectivity in Distilled Language Models
sections.problem: It is unclear what a distilled student model inherits when its teacher carries a backdoor triggered by a rare string that causes a fixed refusal.
sections.method: Holding the trigger fixed, the authors vary only its position (random word boundary versus appended to the instruction) and compare teachers and students on the exact trigger, six control strings, and clean inputs across Qwen2.5, Llama 3.2, and Gemma 3, with 5% of transfer prompts triggered; they also train students on the same prompts without a teacher.
sections.key_result: Randomly inserted triggers became less selective after distillation in all nine teacher-student pipelines, while appended triggers gained selectivity in Qwen and Llama and changed little in Gemma; teacher-free students show much of this is not inherited, with Llama and Gemma students learning an appended backdoor from 150 poisoned examples alone and only Qwen's 0.5B student needing the teacher.
sections.caveat: Findings are limited to three model families and a single fixed trigger type; the abstract reports no aggregate quantitative metrics, and the organization attribution is only probable.
sections.why_it_matters: It argues that backdoor audits should compare teacher and student on the same inputs, probe several trigger positions, and include a teacher-free student baseline.

sections.title: Research Themes
content: Verification and auditing of model behavior beyond raw generation quality
LLM-driven automation of expert engineering workflows
Robustness and safety of model distillation pipelines

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: This week's shortlist pairs an applied LLM agent for engineering design with a safety study of distillation. Both stress verification: one checks optimization outputs at runtime, the other shows that backdoor behavior in students cannot be assumed to mirror the teacher. Organization attributions for both papers are probable author-line matches only and should not be treated as confirmed.
